section.content: Disclosed are aqueous binder compositions comprising at least one long chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of at least 2,000 daltons; a primary crosslinker comprising at least two carboxylic acid groups; and a secondary crosslinker comprising a short chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of less than 2,000 daltons.
公开了水性粘结剂组合物，其包含至少一种具有至少两个羟基和至少2,000道尔顿的数均分子量的长链多元醇；包含至少两个羧酸基团的主交联剂；和包含具有至少两个羟基和小于2,000道尔顿的数均分子量的短链多元醇的副交联剂。

Aqueous binder compositionRELATED APPLICATIONS

This application claims priority and benefit from U.S. provisional application No. 62/831,222 filed on 9/4/2019, the entire contents of which are incorporated herein by reference.

Background

Aqueous binder compositions are conventionally used to form woven and nonwoven fibrous products, such as insulation products (insulation products), composite products, wood fiber boards, and the like. Insulation products, such as fiberglass and mineral wool insulation products, are typically manufactured as follows: fiberizing a molten composition of polymer, glass or other mineral and spinning fine fibers from a fiberizing apparatus, such as a rotary spinning machine. To form the insulation product, the fibers produced by the rotary spinner are drawn downward from the spinner toward a conveyor by a blower. As the fibers move downward, binder material is sprayed onto the fibers and the fibers are collected in a high loft, continuous blanket on a conveyor. The binder material imparts resiliency to the insulation product for recovery after packaging and provides rigidity and handleability so that the insulation product can be handled and applied to the insulation cavity of a building as needed. The binder composition also provides protection for the fibers from interfilament abrasion and promotes compatibility between individual fibers. The blanket containing the binder-coated fibers is then passed through a curing oven and the binder is cured to set the blanket to the desired thickness.

After the binder has cured, the fibrous insulation may be cut to certain lengths to form individual insulation products, and the insulation products may be packaged for shipment to a customer's location.

Fiberglass insulation products made in this manner can be provided in a variety of forms, including batts (batt), blankets, and boards (heated and compressed batts) for different applications. As the binder coated fibrous batt exits the forming chamber, it will tend to expand due to the elasticity of the glass fibers. The expanded batt is then typically conveyed to and through a curing oven where heated air is passed through the insulation product to cure the binder. In addition to curing the binder, the insulation product may be compressed with a squeegee or roller within a curing oven to produce the desired size and surface finish on the resulting blanket, batt or board product.

Phenol-formaldehyde (PF) binder compositions and PF resins (PUF resins) extended with urea are traditionally used to make fiberglass insulation products. Insulation boards, also referred to as "heavy density" products, such as ceiling tiles, duct wraps, duct liners, and the like, have utilized phenol-formaldehyde binder technology to produce heavy density products that are inexpensive and have acceptable physical and mechanical properties. Formaldehyde binders, however, emit undesirable emissions during the manufacture of fiberglass insulation.

As an alternative to formaldehyde-based binders, certain formaldehyde-free formulations have been developed for use as binders in fiberglass insulation products. However, one of the challenges in developing suitable alternatives is to identify formulations that have comparable mechanical and physical properties while avoiding undesirable properties (e.g., discoloration). Such property challenges include hot/wet performance, stiffness, bond strength, processability (viscosity, cutting, sanding, edge painting) and achieving a light color without yellowing.

Thus, there remains a need for environmentally friendly, formaldehyde-free binder compositions for preparing insulation products without experiencing loss of physical and mechanical properties.

Disclosure of Invention

Various exemplary aspects of the present inventive concept relate to an aqueous binder composition comprising at least 35 wt% of a crosslinker comprising at least two carboxylic acid groups, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition, 0.1 to 50.0 wt% of at least one long chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of at least 2,000 daltons, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition; and optionally, at least one short chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of less than 2,000 daltons. The binder composition, once cured, comprises up to 6.0 wt% of water soluble material.

In some exemplary embodiments, the crosslinking agent is a polymeric polycarboxylic acid, such as a homopolymer or copolymer of acrylic acid. The crosslinker may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 50 to 85 wt.%, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition. In some exemplary embodiments, the crosslinking agent is present in the binder composition in an amount of 65 wt% to 80 wt%, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition.

In various exemplary embodiments, the short-chain polyol is present in the binder composition in an amount of 1.0 wt.% to 50 wt.%, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition. In various exemplary embodiments, the short chain polyol comprises one or more of a sugar alcohol, 2-bis (hydroxymethyl) propionic acid, tris (hydroxymethyl) propane, and a short chain alkanolamine. When the short chain polyol comprises a sugar alcohol, the sugar alcohol may be selected from glycerol, erythritol, arabitol, xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol, mannitol, iditol, isomalt, lactitol, cellubitol, palatinitol, maltotriol, syrups thereof and mixtures thereof.

In some exemplary embodiments, the long chain polyol is selected from partially or fully hydrolyzed polyvinyl alcohol and polyvinyl acetate. The long chain polyol may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 1 to 30 wt%, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition.

In various exemplary embodiments, the ratio of long chain polyol to short chain polyol is from 1/50 to 20/1.

In various exemplary embodiments, the binder composition has a water soluble material content of up to 5.0 wt% after curing.

Other exemplary aspects of the present inventive concept relate to an aqueous binder composition comprising 0.1 to 50 wt% of at least one long chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of at least 2,000 daltons, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition; at least 35 wt% of a crosslinker comprising at least two carboxylic acid groups, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition; and 1.0 to 50 wt% of at least one short chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of less than 2,000 daltons. The adhesive composition includes a ratio of molar equivalents of carboxylic acid groups, anhydride groups, or salts thereof to molar equivalents of hydroxyl groups of from 1/0.05 to 1/20, and a ratio of the long chain polyol to the short chain polyol of from 1/50 to 20/1.

Other exemplary aspects of the present inventive concept relate to a fibrous product comprising a plurality of randomly oriented fibers and an aqueous binder composition at least partially coating the fibers. The binder composition may comprise at least 35 wt% of a crosslinker comprising at least two carboxylic acid groups, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition, from 0.1 to 50.0 wt% of at least one long chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of at least 2,000 daltons, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition; and optionally, at least one short chain polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of less than 2,000 daltons. The binder composition, once cured, comprises up to 6.0 wt% of water soluble material.

The fibers of the insulation product may include one or more of mineral fibers, natural fibers, and synthetic fibers, and in some embodiments, the fibers include glass fibers.

In some exemplary embodiments, the fibrous product comprises any of an insulation product, a nonwoven mat, a particle board, a ceiling board (ceiling board), a channel board (product board), and the like.

Many other aspects, advantages and/or features of the general inventive concept will become more apparent from the following detailed description of exemplary embodiments and the accompanying drawings as filed herewith.

Detailed Description

Unless defined otherwise, all technical and scientific terms used herein have the same meaning as commonly understood by one of ordinary skill in the art to which these exemplary embodiments belong. The terminology used in the description herein is for the purpose of describing exemplary embodiments only and is not intended to be limiting of exemplary embodiments. Accordingly, the general inventive concept is not intended to be limited to the specific embodiments shown herein. Although other methods and materials similar or equivalent to those described herein can be used in the practice or testing of the present invention, the preferred methods and materials are described herein.

As used in the specification and the appended claims, the singular forms "a", "an", and "the" are intended to include the plural forms as well, unless the context clearly indicates otherwise.

Unless otherwise indicated, all numbers expressing quantities of ingredients, chemical and molecular properties, reaction conditions, and so forth, used in the specification and claims are to be understood as being modified in all instances by the term "about". Accordingly, unless indicated to the contrary, the numerical parameters set forth in the following specification and attached claims are approximations that may vary depending upon the desired properties sought to be obtained by exemplary embodiments of the present invention. At the very least, and not as an attempt to limit the application of the doctrine of equivalents to the number of equivalents, each numerical parameter should at least be construed in light of the number of reported significant digits and ordinary rounding approaches.

Notwithstanding that the numerical ranges and parameters setting forth the broad scope of the exemplary embodiments are approximations, the numerical values set forth in the specific examples are reported as precisely as possible. Any numerical value, however, inherently contains certain errors necessarily resulting from the standard deviation found in their respective testing measurements. Every numerical range given throughout this specification and claims will include every narrower numerical range that falls within such broader numerical range, as if such narrower numerical ranges were all expressly written herein.

The present disclosure relates to formaldehyde-free aqueous binder compositions for use in the manufacture of insulation products having comparable or improved mechanical and physical properties compared to products made with conventional formaldehyde-based binder compositions. The formaldehyde-free binder composition can be used in the manufacture of fibrous insulation products made with the cured formaldehyde-free binder and related products, such as thin fibrous reinforcing mats (hereinafter collectively referred to collectively as fiber-reinforced products) and fiberglass or mineral wool products, particularly fiberglass or mineral wool insulation products. Other products may include composite products, wood fiberboard products, metal building insulation, pipe insulation, ceilings, ceiling tiles, "heavy density" products such as ceilings, pipe wraps, pipe liners, and "light density" products. Additional fibrous products include nonwoven fibrous mats and particle boards, as well as composite products made therefrom.

In some exemplary embodiments, the formaldehyde-free aqueous binder composition comprises at least one primary crosslinker and at least one secondary crosslinker comprising at least one short-chain polyol and at least one long-chain polyol.

The primary crosslinker can be any compound suitable for crosslinking a polyol. In exemplary embodiments, the primary crosslinker has a number average molecular weight of greater than 90 daltons, from 90 daltons to 10,000 daltons, or from 190 daltons to 5,000 daltons. In some exemplary embodiments, the crosslinking agent has a number average molecular weight of 2,000 daltons to 5,000 daltons, or 4,000 daltons. Non-limiting examples of suitable crosslinking agents include materials having one or more carboxylic acid groups (-COOH), such as polycarboxylic acids (and salts thereof), anhydrides, monomeric and polymeric polycarboxylic acids and anhydrides (i.e., mixed anhydrides), and homopolymers or copolymers of acrylic acid, such as polyacrylic acid (and salts thereof) and polyacrylic acid-based resins, such as QR-1629S and Acumer9932, both commercially available from Dow Chemical Company. Acumer9932 is a polyacrylic acid/sodium hypophosphite resin with a molecular weight of 4000 and a sodium hypophosphite content of 6-7 wt%. QR-1629S is a polyacrylic acid/glycerol mixture.

In some cases, the primary crosslinker may be pre-neutralized with a neutralizing agent. Such neutralizing agents may include organic and/or inorganic bases such as sodium hydroxide, ammonium hydroxide, and diethylamine, as well as any kind of primary, secondary, or tertiary amines (including alkanolamines). In various exemplary embodiments, the neutralizing agent may include at least one of sodium hydroxide and triethanolamine.

In some exemplary embodiments, the primary crosslinker is present in the aqueous binder composition at least 50 wt.%, including but not limited to at least 55 wt.%, at least 60 wt.%, at least 63 wt.%, at least 65 wt.%, at least 70 wt.%, at least 73 wt.%, at least 75 wt.%, at least 78 wt.%, and at least 80 wt.%, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition. In some exemplary embodiments, the primary crosslinker is present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount of 50 wt.% to 85 wt.%, including but not limited to 60 wt.% to 80 wt.%, 62 wt.% to 78 wt.%, and 65 wt.% to 75 wt.%, including all endpoints and subsets therebetween, based on the total solids content of the aqueous binder composition.

In some exemplary embodiments, the long chain polyol comprises a polyol having at least two hydroxyl groups and a number average molecular weight of at least 2,000 daltons, for example, a molecular weight of 3,000 daltons to 4,000 daltons. In some exemplary embodiments, the long chain polyol comprises one or more polymeric polyols, such as polyvinyl alcohol, polyvinyl acetate, which may be partially or fully hydrolyzed, or mixtures thereof. Illustratively, when partially hydrolyzed polyvinyl acetate serves as the polyhydroxy component, 80% -89% hydrolyzed polyvinyl acetate may be used, for example385(Kuraray America, Inc.) and SevolTM502(Sekisui Specialty Chemicals America, LLC), both 85% ((L.) (385) And 88% (Selvol)TM502) And (4) hydrolyzing.

The long chain polyol may be present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount up to 50 wt% total solids, including but not limited to up to 40 wt%, 35 wt%, 30 wt%, 28 wt%, 25 wt%, 20 wt%, 18 wt%, 15 wt%, and 13 wt% total solids. In some exemplary embodiments, the long chain polyol is present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount of 0.1 to 50 wt% total solids, including but not limited to 0.5 wt% to 30 wt%, 1 wt% to 20 wt%, 5 wt% to 18 wt%, and 7 wt% to 15 wt% total solids, including all endpoints and subsets therebetween.

Optionally, the aqueous binder composition comprises a secondary crosslinker, such as a short-chain polyol. The short chain polyol may comprise a water soluble compound having a molecular weight of less than 2,000 daltons (including less than 750 daltons, less than 500 daltons) and having a plurality of hydroxyl groups (-OH). Suitable short chain polyol components include sugar alcohols, 2-bis (hydroxymethyl) propionic acid (bis-MPA), tris (hydroxymethyl) propane (TMP), pentaerythritol and short chain alkanolamines, such as triethanolamine. In some exemplary embodiments, the short chain polyol acts as a viscosity reducing agent that disrupts intra-and intermolecular hydrogen bonds between long chain polyol molecules (e.g., polyvinyl alcohol) and thereby reduces the viscosity of the composition. However, since these small chain polyol molecules have a similar structure to long chain polyols, they can react similarly to the cross-linking agent, and therefore they do not adversely affect the binder and product properties.

Sugar alcohols are understood as meaning compounds which are obtained when the aldehyde or ketone groups of a sugar are reduced, for example by hydrogenation, to the corresponding hydroxyl groups. The starting sugar may be selected from monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, as well as mixtures of these products, such as syrup, molasses and starch hydrolysates. The starting sugar may also be a dehydrated form of the sugar. Although sugar alcohols are very similar to the corresponding starting sugars, they are not sugars. Thus, for example, sugar alcohols do not have reducing power and cannot participate in the maillard reaction typical of reducing sugars. In some exemplary embodiments, the sugar alcohol comprises glycerol, erythritol, arabitol, xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol, mannitol, iditol, isomalt, lactitol, cellubitol, palatinitol, maltotriol, syrups thereof, and mixtures thereof. In various exemplary embodiments, the sugar alcohol is selected from the group consisting of glycerol, sorbitol, xylitol, and mixtures thereof. In some exemplary embodiments, the secondary crosslinker is a dimeric or oligomeric condensation product of a sugar alcohol. In various exemplary embodiments, the condensation product of the sugar alcohol is isosorbide. In some exemplary embodiments, the sugar alcohol is a diol or glycol.

In some exemplary embodiments, the short chain polyol is present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount up to 50 wt% total solids, including but not limited to up to 40 wt%, 35 wt%, 30 wt%, 25 wt%, 20 wt%, 18 wt%, 15 wt%, 13 wt%, 11 wt%, and 10 wt% total solids. In some exemplary embodiments, the short-chain polyol is present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount of 0 to 50 wt% total solids, including but not limited to 2 wt% to 45 wt%, 1 wt% to 35 wt%, 5 wt% to 30 wt%, 7 wt% to 27 wt%, and 10 wt% to 25 wt% total solids, including all endpoints and subsets therebetween.

In various exemplary embodiments, the long chain polyol, the crosslinking agent, and the small chain polyol are present in amounts such that the ratio of the number of molar equivalents of carboxylic acid groups, anhydride groups, or salts thereof to the number of molar equivalents of hydroxyl groups is from 1/0.05 to 1/20, including from 1/0.3 to 1/10, such as from 1/0.1 to 1/5.0, from 1/0.3 to 1/3, and from 1/0.4 to 1/2.5. However, it has been surprisingly found that the ratio of long chain polyol to short chain polyol based on the molar equivalents of hydroxyl groups within such a ratio affects the properties of the binder composition, such as the tensile strength and water solubility of the binder after curing. For example, it has been found that a ratio of long chain polyol to short chain polyol of between 1/50 and 20/1, such as between 1/20 and 10/1, or between 1/10 and 5/1-2/11/1 provides a desirable balance of mechanical and physical properties. In various exemplary embodiments, the ratio of long chain polyol to short chain polyol is about 1/30. The ratio of long chain polyol to short chain polyol can be optimized such that specific properties are optimized as required by the end use application. For example, reducing the concentration of long chain polyol can reduce the tensile strength of products formed with the binder composition. However, lowering the long chain polyol can affect other properties, such as physical properties. Thus, a balance between the various properties is unexpectedly achieved within the ratios disclosed herein.

It has been surprisingly found that although long chain polyols such as polyvinyl alcohol generally have the highest viscosity of all binder ingredients, the addition of a small amount of long chain polyol actually reduces the overall binder viscosity. In some exemplary embodiments, the addition of a small amount of long chain polyol (0.1 wt% to less than 20 wt%) reduces the viscosity of the binder solution by up to 50% based on the viscosity of the binder composition excluding the long chain polyol. It has also been found that the addition of a small amount of long chain polyol increases the tensile/LOI strength up to 40% at ambient and hot-humid conditions compared to the tensile/LOI strength of an adhesive composition without the long chain polyol.

Optionally, the aqueous binder composition may include an esterification catalyst, also referred to as a cure accelerator. The catalyst may include inorganic salts, lewis acids (i.e., aluminum chloride or boron trifluoride), bronsted acids (i.e., sulfuric acid, p-toluenesulfonic acid, and boric acid), organometallic complexes (i.e., lithium carboxylates, sodium carboxylates), and/or lewis bases (i.e., polyethyleneimine, diethylamine, or triethylamine). In addition, the catalyst may include an alkali metal salt of a phosphorus-containing organic acid; in particular alkali metal salts of phosphoric acid, hypophosphorous acid or polyphosphoric acids. Examples of such phosphorus-containing catalysts include, but are not limited to, sodium hypophosphite, sodium phosphate, potassium phosphate, disodium pyrophosphate, tetrasodium pyrophosphate, sodium tripolyphosphate, sodium hexametaphosphate, potassium phosphate, potassium tripolyphosphate, sodium trimetaphosphate, sodium tetrametaphosphate, and mixtures thereof. In addition, the catalyst or cure accelerator may be a fluoroborate compound, such as fluoroboric acid, sodium tetrafluoroborate, potassium tetrafluoroborate, calcium tetrafluoroborate, magnesium tetrafluoroborate, zinc tetrafluoroborate, ammonium tetrafluoroborate, and mixtures thereof. Further, the catalyst may be a mixture of a phosphorus-containing compound and a fluoroborate compound. Other sodium salts such as sodium sulfate, sodium nitrate, sodium carbonate may also or alternatively be used as catalysts.

The catalyst may be present in the aqueous binder composition in an amount of 0 wt% to 10 wt% of the total solids in the binder composition, including but not limited to an amount of 1 wt% to 5 wt%, or 2 wt% to 4.5 wt%, or 2.8 wt% to 4.0 wt%, or 3.0 wt% to 3.8 wt%.

Optionally, the aqueous binder composition may contain at least one coupling agent. In at least one exemplary embodiment, the coupling agent is a silane coupling agent. The coupling agent(s) may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 0.01 wt% to 5 wt%, 0.01 wt% to 2.5 wt%, 0.05 wt% to 1.5 wt%, or 0.1 wt% to 1.0 wt% of the total solids in the binder composition.

Non-limiting examples of silane coupling agents that may be used in the binder composition may be characterized by the functional groups alkyl, aryl, amino, epoxy, vinyl, methacryloxy, ureido, isocyanate, and mercapto. In exemplary embodiments, the silane coupling agent(s) include silanes containing one or more nitrogen atoms having one or more functional groups such as amine (primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary), amino, imino, amido, imino, ureido, or isocyanato groups. Specific non-limiting examples of suitable silane coupling agents include, but are not limited to, aminosilanes (e.g., triethoxyaminopropyl silane, 3-aminopropyl-triethoxysilane, and 3-aminopropyl-trihydroxysilane), epoxytrialkoxysilanes (e.g., 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane, and 3-glycidoxypropyltriethoxysilane), methacryloxysilanes (e.g., 3-methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane, and 3-methacryloxypropyltriethoxysilane), hydrocycloxysilanes, aminotrialkoxysilanes, epoxytrihydroxysilanes, methacrylotrihydroxysilanes, and/or hydrocycloxysilanes. In one or more exemplary embodiments, the silane is an aminosilane, such as gamma-aminopropyltriethoxysilane.

Optionally, the aqueous binder composition may include a processing aid. The processing aid is not particularly limited as long as the processing aid functions to promote processing of fiber formation and orientation. Processing aids can be used to improve binder application distribution uniformity, reduce binder viscosity, increase ramp height after forming (ramp height), improve vertical weight distribution uniformity, and/or accelerate binder dewatering during forming and oven curing. The processing aid may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 0 to 10 wt%, 0.1 wt% to 5.0 wt%, or 0.3 wt% to 2.0 wt%, or 0.5 wt% to 1.0 wt%, based on the total solids content in the binder composition. In some exemplary embodiments, the aqueous binder composition is substantially free or completely free of any processing aids.

Examples of processing aids include defoamers, such as emulsions and/or dispersions of mineral, paraffin or vegetable oils; a dispersion of Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) fluid, and silica that has been hydrophobated with polydimethylsiloxane or other materials. Other processing aids may include particles made from amide waxes, such as Ethylene Bis Stearamide (EBS) or hydrophobized silica. Additional processing aids that may be used in the binder composition are surfactants. One or more surfactants may be included in the binder composition to aid in binder atomization, wetting, and interfacial adhesion.

The surfactant is not particularly limited, and includes surfactants such as, but not limited to, ionic surfactants (e.g., sulfates, sulfonates, phosphates, and carboxylates); sulfates (e.g., alkyl sulfates, ammonium lauryl sulfate, sodium lauryl sulfate (SDS), alkyl ether sulfates, sodium laureth sulfate, and sodium myristyl polyether sulfate); amphoteric surfactants (e.g., alkyl betaines, such as lauryl betaine); sulfonates (e.g., dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, perfluorooctane sulfonate, perfluorobutane sulfonate, and alkylbenzene sulfonate); phosphate esters (e.g., alkyl aryl ether phosphate esters and alkyl ether phosphate esters); carboxylates (e.g., alkyl carboxylates, fatty acid salts (soaps), sodium stearate, sodium lauroyl sarcosinate, carboxylate fluorosurfactants, perfluorononanoates, and perfluorooctanoates); cationic (e.g., alkylamine salts, such as laurylamine acetate); pH-dependent surfactants (primary, secondary or tertiary amines); permanently charged quaternary ammonium cations (e.g., alkyltrimethylammonium salts, cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, cetyltrimethylammonium chloride, cetylpyridinium chlorideAnd benzethonium chloride); and zwitterionic surfactants, quaternary ammonium salts (e.g., lauryl trimethyl ammonium chloride and alkyl benzyl dimethyl ammonium chloride), and polyoxyethylene alkylamines.

Suitable nonionic surfactants that can be used in conjunction with the binder composition include polyethers (e.g., ethylene oxide and propylene oxide condensates that include straight and branched chain alkyl and alkaryl polyethylene and polypropylene glycol ethers and thioethers); alkylphenoxypoly (ethyleneoxy) ethanol having an alkyl group containing from 7 to 18 carbon atoms and having from 4 to 240 ethyleneoxy units (e.g., heptylphenoxypoly (ethyleneoxy) ethanol and nonylphenoxypoly (ethyleneoxy) ethanol); polyoxyalkylene derivatives of hexitols including sorbitan, mannitan and mannitan; partial long-chain fatty acid esters (e.g., polyoxyalkylene derivatives of sorbitan monolaurate, sorbitan monopalmitate, sorbitan monostearate, sorbitan tristearate, sorbitan monooleate, and sorbitan trioleate); a condensate of ethylene oxide with a hydrophobic base formed by condensing propylene oxide with propylene glycol; sulfur-containing condensates (e.g., those prepared by condensing ethylene oxide with higher alkyl mercaptans (such as nonyl, dodecyl, or tetradecyl mercaptan) or with alkylthiophenols in which the alkyl group contains from 6 to 15 carbon atoms); ethylene oxide derivatives of long chain carboxylic acids (e.g., lauric, myristic, palmitic, and oleic acids, such as tall oil fatty acids); ethylene oxide derivatives of long chain alcohols (e.g., octanol, decanol, lauryl alcohol, or cetyl alcohol); and ethylene oxide/propylene oxide copolymers.

In at least one exemplary embodiment, the surfactant comprises one or more of the following: dynol 607 (which is 2,5,8, 11-tetramethyl-6-dodecyne-5, 8-diol),420、440 and465 (which is an ethoxylated 2,4,7, 9-tetramethyl-5-decyne-4, 7-diol surfactant) (commercially available from Evonik Corporation (Allentown, Pa.)); stanfax (sodium lauryl sulfate), Surfynol465 (ethoxylated 2,4,7, 9-tetramethyl-5-decyne-4, 7-diol), TritonTMGR-PG70 (sodium 1, 4-bis (2-ethylhexyl) sulfosuccinate) and TritonTMCF-10 (poly (oxy-1, 2-ethanediyl), α - (phenylmethyl) - ω - (1,1,3, 3-tetramethylbutyl) phenoxy).

The surfactant may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 0 to 10 wt%, 0.1 wt% to 5.0 wt%, or 0.3 wt% to 2.0 wt%, or 0.5 wt% to 1.0 wt%, based on the total solids content in the binder composition.

The binder composition may also contain organic and/or inorganic acids and bases as pH adjusting agents in amounts sufficient to adjust the pH to the desired level. The pH may be adjusted depending on the intended application to promote compatibility of the components of the binder composition or to work with various types of fibers. In some exemplary embodiments, the pH adjuster is used to adjust the pH of the binder composition to an acidic pH. Examples of suitable acidic pH adjusters include inorganic acids such as, but not limited to, sulfuric acid, phosphoric acid, and boric acid, and organic acids such as p-toluenesulfonic acid, monocarboxylic acids, or polycarboxylic acids such as, but not limited to, citric acid, acetic acid and anhydrides thereof, adipic acid, oxalic acid, and corresponding salts thereof. Also inorganic salts which may be acid precursors. The acid adjusts the pH and, in some cases, acts as a crosslinking agent, as described above. In other exemplary embodiments, organic and/or inorganic bases may be included to increase the pH of the binder composition. In some exemplary embodiments, the base may be a volatile or non-volatile base. Exemplary volatile bases include, for example, ammonia and alkyl-substituted amines, such as methylamine, ethylamine or 1-aminopropane, dimethylamine and ethylmethylamine. Exemplary non-volatile bases include, for example, sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium carbonate, and tert-butylammonium hydroxide.

The pH adjusting agent may be present in the binder composition in an amount of 0 to 10 wt%, 0.1 wt% to 5.0 wt%, or 0.3 wt% to 2.0 wt%, or 0.5 wt% to 1.0 wt%, based on the total solids content in the binder composition. In some exemplary embodiments, the aqueous binder composition is substantially free or completely free of any pH adjusting agent.

When in the uncured state, the pH of the binder composition may be in the range of 2 to 5, including all amounts and ranges therebetween. In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition, when in an uncured state, has a pH of 2.2 to 4.0, including 2.5 to 3.8 and 2.6 to 3.5. Upon curing, the pH of the binder composition may rise to a pH of at least 6.0, including levels of 6.5 to 7.2 or 6.8 to 7.2.

Optionally, the binder may contain dust inhibitors to reduce or eliminate the presence of inorganic and/or organic particles that may have adverse effects in subsequent manufacture and installation of the insulation material. The dust suppressant may be any conventional mineral oil, mineral oil emulsion, natural or synthetic oil, bio-based oil or lubricant such as, but not limited to, silicone and silicone emulsions, polyethylene glycol, and any petroleum or non-petroleum oil having a high flash point to minimize evaporation of the oil within the oven.

In some exemplary embodiments, the aqueous binder composition comprises up to 10 wt% dust suppressant, including up to 8 wt% or up to 6 wt%. In various exemplary embodiments, the aqueous binder composition comprises 0 wt% to 10 wt% dust suppressant, including 1.0 wt% to 7.0 wt% or 1.5 wt% to 6.5 wt% or 2.0 wt% to 6.0 wt% or 2.5 wt% to 5.8 wt%.

The binder also includes water to dissolve or disperse the active solids for application to the reinforcing fibers. Water may be added in a sufficient amount to dilute the aqueous binder composition to a viscosity suitable for its application to the reinforcing fibers and to achieve the desired solids content on the fibers. It has been found that the binder composition of the present invention can contain lower solids content than conventional binder compositions based on phenol-urea formaldehyde or carbohydrates. In particular, the binder composition may comprise 3 to 35 wt% binder solids, including but not limited to 10 to 30 wt%, 12 to 20 wt%, and 15 to 19 wt% binder solids. Such solids content indicates that the binder composition of the present invention may contain more water than conventional binder compositions. However, due to the high cure rate of the binder composition, the binder can be processed at high ramp moisture levels (3% -30%) and the binder composition requires less cure residence time to remove moisture than conventional binder compositions. The binder content on the product can be measured as Loss On Ignition (LOI). In certain embodiments, the LOI on the glass fibers forming the insulation product is from 0.5% to 50%, including but not limited to from 1% to 25%, from 5% to 19%, and from 4.5% to 17%.

In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition is capable of achieving similar or higher performance than traditional phenolic or starch-hybrid binder compositions having lower LOIs.

In some exemplary embodiments, the aqueous binder composition may further comprise one or more additives, such as coupling agents, extenders, crosslink density enhancers, deodorants, antioxidants, dust suppressants, biocides, moisture repellents, or combinations thereof. Optionally, the binder may include, but is not limited to, dyes, pigments, additional fillers, colorants, UV stabilizers, heat stabilizers, defoamers, emulsifiers, preservatives (e.g., sodium benzoate), corrosion inhibitors, and mixtures thereof. Other additives may be added to the binder composition to improve processing and product performance. Such additives include lubricants, wetting agents, antistatic agents, and/or water repellents. The additive may be present in the binder composition in trace amounts (e.g., <0.1 wt% of the binder composition) to 10 wt% of the total solids in the binder composition.

In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition is formulated to have a reduced level of water soluble material after curing, as determined by extracting the water soluble material with 1000g of deionized water based on 1 gram of binder at room temperature for 2 hours. The higher the level of water soluble material after curing, the more likely the cured material will suffer leaching if/when exposed to water and/or heat/humidity. In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition has up to 6 wt% water soluble material after curing. In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition has less than 5.0 wt% water soluble material after curing, including less than 5.0 wt%, 4.0 wt%, 3.0 wt%, less than 2.5 wt%, less than 2.0 wt%, less than 1.5 wt%, or less than 1.0 wt%. It has been found that reducing the level of water soluble material after curing to up to 6.0 wt% improves the tensile strength of the binder composition compared to other similar binder compositions having greater than 6.0 wt% water soluble material after curing.

The amount of water-soluble material remaining in the binder composition after curing may be determined, at least in part, by the amount of carboxylic acid groups in the binder. In particular, an excess of acid groups increases the water-soluble content, resulting in an increase in water-soluble material after curing. As shown in Table 3 below, comparative examples 1 and 2 have highly acidic COOH/OH ratios, resulting in an unacceptably high percentage of water soluble material after curing. In contrast, the percentage of water-soluble material remaining after curing was significantly reduced when the COOH/OH ratio was 1/0.1 or less.

It has further been found that the total polyol content should contain at least 10 wt% of one or more short chain polyols to produce a binder composition having an acceptably low level (e.g., up to 6 wt%) of water soluble material after curing. This is particularly surprising because, in general, short-chain polyols such as sorbitol have a high water solubility. Thus, it might be expected that increasing the sorbitol content would increase the amount of water-soluble material in the binder composition rather than decrease it.

In some exemplary embodiments, the binder composition has a viscosity of 400cP or less at 30% solids, including a viscosity of 300cP or less at 30% solids, 200cP or less at 30% solids, 175cP or less at 30% solids, and 150cP or less at 30% solids. In various exemplary embodiments, the viscosity of the binder composition is at most 250cP or less at 30% solids.

The fibrous product of the present disclosure comprises a plurality of randomly oriented fibers. In certain exemplary embodiments, the plurality of randomly oriented fibers are mineral fibers including, but not limited to, glass fibers, glass wool fibers, mineral wool fibers, slag wool fibers, asbestos fibers, ceramic fibers, metal fibers, and combinations thereof.

Optionally, other reinforcing fibers may be used in the nonwoven fibrous mat, such as natural and/or synthetic fibers, such as carbon, polyester, polyethylene terephthalate, polypropylene, polyamide, aramid, and/or polyaramid fibers. The term "natural fiber" as used herein refers to plant fiber extracted from any part of a plant, including but not limited to the stem, seeds, leaves, roots, or phloem. Examples of natural fibers suitable for use as the reinforcing fiber material include wood fibers, cellulosic fibers, straw, wood chips, wood strands, cotton, jute, bamboo, ramie, bagasse, hemp, coir, linen, kenaf, sisal, flax, sisal, and combinations thereof. The fibrous insulation products may be formed entirely of one type of fiber, or they may be formed from a combination of multiple types of fibers. For example, the insulation product may be formed from various combinations of glass fibers or various combinations of different inorganic fibers and/or natural fibers, depending on the desired application. In certain exemplary embodiments, the insulation product is formed entirely of glass fibers.

Example 2

Binder compositions having different COOH/OH and long chain polyol/short chain polyol ratios were used to form nonwoven glass fiber Binder Impregnated Filter (BIF) sheets having a width of 9.5mm, a thickness of 0.5mm, and a length of 97 mm. The nonwoven glass fiber BIF sheet was cured at 425 ° F for 3 minutes and 30 seconds. The tensile strength, Loss On Ignition (LOI) and tensile strength of each sample were determined under ambient conditions and steam ("hot/humid") conditions divided by the LOI (tensile strength/LOI). Tensile strength was measured using an Instron (tensile speed 2 inches/minute). The LOI of the reinforcing fibers is the weight loss experienced by the fibers after they are heated to a temperature sufficient to burn or pyrolyze the binder composition from the fibers. LOI is measured according to the procedure described in TAPPI T-1013OM06, Loss on orientation of fiber glass mats (2006). To create a hot/humid environment, the filter sheet is placed in an autoclave at 240 ° F at a pressure of 400psi to 500psi for 60 minutes.

As shown in FIG. 2, the tensile/LOI appears to generally increase under ambient and hot/humid conditions as the proportion of short chain polyol in the composition increases (within a COOH/OH ratio of 1/0.1). This relationship appears to be consistent with the level of residual hydrosoluble in the composition after curing (FIG. 3). Figure 3 shows that as the proportion of short chain polyol increases, the percentage of water soluble material in the composition after curing decreases.

These relationships continue when the COOH/OH ratio is adjusted to 1/1.5, as shown in FIGS. 4 and 5. It is noteworthy, however, that the percentage of water-soluble material remaining in the composition after curing is significantly lower in this COOH/OH range. For example, even in compositions lacking any short chain polyol, the percentage of water soluble material is less than 8.0%, and after some short chain polyol is added, the percentage drops below 5.0%.

However, when the COOH/OH ratio was adjusted to 1/0.5, 1/0.1, and 1/1, the tensile strength of ambient and hot/humid conditions remained relatively constant regardless of the long chain/short chain polyol ratio, although the percentage of water-soluble material similarly decreased with increasing short chain polyol ratio. See fig. 6 to 9. However, it should be noted that when the COOH/OH ratio is 1/0.5, the highest ambient tensile strength/LOI (44 and 45 tensile strength/LOI, respectively) is exhibited at long chain/short chain polyol ratios of 0.5/0.5 and 0.3/0.7.

Fig. 10 shows the transfer of tensile/LOI for filters impregnated with binder compositions having different COOH/OH ratios from 1/0.1 to 1/10. As shown, the optimum stretch/LOI under ambient and hot/humid conditions can be seen when the COOH/OH ratio is not too low or too high. At too high or too low a COOH/OH ratio, the tensile/LOI under hot/humid conditions is affected, which leads to insufficient strength properties.
